clue.text: Get Listener misdirection at last

parts.note: an ear is what listens, so it is a listener

indicators.note: points to the final letter of the word misdirection

explanation.surface: A puzzler complains that the Listener crossword finally steered them wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The Listener is a famously hard newspaper crossword, which sets up the misdirection; here it is just an ear.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn money is to get it in return for work, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Recognise one with all-consuming interests being upset

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means the word is turned upside down, read from bottom to top

parts.note: a wonk is someone obsessed with the details of a subject

explanation.surface: Someone spots an obsessive whose passions have been thrown into turmoil.
explanation.definitionFit: To know someone or something can mean to identify it on sight, a synonym of recognising.

clue.text: Boatman replaces leader of house in Slough with fixed gaze

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for the past-tense verb; it fits if 'with' is read as a link

indicators.note: one piece takes the place of another inside the word for slough

parts.note: to slough is to shed, as a snake does its skin

indicators.note: the leading letter of the word house is the one swapped out

parts.note: a tar is a sailor, and the setter's own pseudonym is Boatman

explanation.surface: The setter turns up in an English town and gets stared at.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the Berkshire town; it is the verb meaning to cast off. The definition is an adverb phrase, so read it as 'looked with fixed gaze' for the swap to work.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who stared looked steadily and intently, without moving their eyes away.

clue.text: Skip Wee Stinker, inverting riddle's outer limits

parts.note: a scamp is a mischievous little rascal, a wee stinker

indicators.note: the two letters picked from riddle are put in the opposite order
takes just the first and last letters of riddle's, ignoring the possessive

explanation.surface: Someone tells a little rascal to clear off, turning a riddle inside out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee Stinker' reads like a rude nickname, but it is one unit for a small rascal; the possessive on riddle's is ignored when taking its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To scamper is to run or skip about playfully with quick light steps.

clue.text: About one oddly intense Genius

indicators.note: about means around and is used here alongside oddly to say the letters are rearranged
the letters of intense with one added are put together in an odd, jumbled order

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A description of a remarkably bright person who is unusually intense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' looks like a request for odd letters; it is an anagram signal over INTENSE plus I.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein's name is used as a byword for a brilliant mind, so an einstein is a genius.

clue.text: Certain old penniless escort on an 'orse

indicators.note: without d, the abbreviation for the old British penny

parts.note: a guard is an escort protecting someone
a steed is a horse; dropping the h of horse is mimicked by dropping the first letter of steed

explanation.surface: A Cockney-sounding picture of a broke old bodyguard riding a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: D stood for the old penny in pre-decimal British money. The apostrophe in 'orse shows a dropped first letter, so STEED loses its S to give TEED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something guaranteed is assured and sure to happen, so certain.

clue.text: Release slow Orwellian nurse

parts.note: in the Newspeak of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, unfast replaces slow
EN is the abbreviation for enrolled nurse

explanation.surface: A sluggish nurse from a dystopian novel is set free.
explanation.walkthrough: Newspeak builds words with un- in place of opposites, so slow becomes unfast.
explanation.definitionFit: To unfasten a clasp or strap is to undo it, letting it go free.

clue.text: Boatman not featuring in Enigmatic Variations is attractive

indicators.note: variations on a theme rearrange its material, so these letters are reshuffled
says the setter's letter is missing from the rearranged word

parts.note: the setter, Boatman, refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: Elgar's Enigma Variations are described as appealing even without the setter's involvement.
explanation.walkthrough: Take one I out of ENIGMATIC and rearrange the rest. Setters often call themselves I, so Boatman is that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnetic personality draws people in, so magnetic means attractive both literally and figuratively.

clue.text: Like to monitor typos in Guardian? No way!

indicators.note: typing errors scramble the letters of the word they sit in
says letters are taken away from the scrambled word

parts.note: RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: Someone who enjoys spotting mistakes in the Guardian is told firmly it won't happen.
explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian is known for its typos. 'Like to' is the old sense of similar to: an iguana is a lizard resembling a monitor lizard.
explanation.definitionFit: Iguanas and monitors are both large lizards, so one is akin to the other.

clue.text: A curse, deleting one article after another

definitions.note: A is a standard abbreviation for answer, as in Q and A

parts.note: an is another indefinite article

indicators.note: says a letter is taken out of the word for curse

parts.note: to curse is to swear
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A grammar puzzle about swearing and removing articles one by one.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the lone opening A, the abbreviation in Q and A.
explanation.definitionFit: In question-and-answer notation the single letter A stands for the reply to a question.

clue.text: 'Make do with less': politician ousted to go downhill fast

indicators.note: an ousted politician is removed, so these letters are thrown out

parts.note: to skimp is to economise, making do with less
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: An austerity slogan, then a politician thrown out and declining rapidly.
explanation.definitionFit: To ski is to slide down snowy slopes at speed, literally going downhill fast.

clue.text: Abuse from security service, apparently a special experience

parts.note: MI5 is the British security service, and MI5 looks like MIS
a treat is something specially enjoyable

explanation.surface: Someone claims their ill-treatment by the security services was a real treat.
explanation.walkthrough: MI5 is Britain's domestic security service; 'apparently' says the 5 is read as the letter S it resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: To mistreat someone is to handle them badly or cruelly, a synonym of abuse.

clue.text: Second of second; second page; second sight

indicators.note: asks for the letter in second place of the following word

explanation.surface: A list of things all called second, ending in clairvoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: The word second does four jobs: its second letter, its abbreviation S, and part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Extrasensory perception is the supposed power of sensing things beyond normal perception, also called second sight.

clue.text: Enjoyed Independent: emerged with no content corrected

indicators.note: each word loses its insides, leaving only the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone liked the Independent newspaper but came away with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Independent is a British newspaper, one of several papers named in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Edited text has been revised and its errors fixed by an editor.

clue.text: Rambling hesitation and bluster

parts.note: er is the sound of someone hesitating
a rant is loud, blustering talk

explanation.surface: A description of a waffling speaker who hesitates and then blusters.
explanation.definitionFit: Errant means wandering or straying, as a knight errant roams in search of adventure.

clue.text: The officer in charge preceding disloyal person in command, claiming divine authority

indicators.note: the pieces before it come ahead of the abbreviation for in command

parts.note: taken as written
OC is the military abbreviation for officer commanding or in charge
a rat is someone who betrays their side
IC is the abbreviation for in charge or in command

explanation.surface: A traitor in charge of the army presents himself as ruling by God's will.
explanation.definitionFit: A theocratic state is governed by priests or rulers who claim to rule on behalf of God.

clue.text: Forever and always, including time with tiny changes

indicators.note: the word for always holds the time abbreviation inside it

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, always

indicators.note: the letters of tiny undergo changes, being rearranged

explanation.surface: A romantic promise of endless love, oddly qualified by small adjustments.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternity means endless time, and 'for an eternity' is a noun sense of forever.

clue.text: Challenges again from different setters

indicators.note: a different arrangement of the letters of setters

explanation.surface: Fresh challenges come from a new set of crossword compilers.
explanation.definitionFit: To retest is to test once more, putting someone through a second challenge.

clue.text: Times creates puzzle that's rather dry

indicators.note: to puzzle means to confuse, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as times

explanation.surface: The Times newspaper sets a puzzle that is a bit dull.
explanation.walkthrough: Times looks like the newspaper; it is the multiplication sign X.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra sec is a label for champagne or sparkling wine meaning medium dry, less dry than brut.

clue.text: Almost domesticated some pigs by the sound of drums

indicators.note: the word for domesticated stops just short of its last letter

parts.note: a tame animal has been domesticated

indicators.note: the word for pigs is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: boars are male pigs

explanation.surface: Pigs that are nearly tame are making a drumming noise.
explanation.walkthrough: BOURS sounds like BOARS in a British accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A tambour is a small drum, so tambours is a plural noun for drums.

clue.text: OneNote audio input extension

indicators.note: audio is about sound, so the pieces are heard and not spelt

parts.note: one is AN, and a note is a TENNER, a ten-pound note

explanation.surface: A tech request for a sound plug-in to Microsoft's OneNote software.
explanation.walkthrough: OneNote looks like the software; it splits into one and note. A tenner is a British ten-pound note. AN TENNER spoken in a British accent sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An antenna is an aerial, a rod that extends out to pick up incoming signals for a receiver.

clue.text: See 14
Some really do by nature become uplifted by Everyman

indicators.note: in a down clue, uplifted means read from bottom to top
says only part of the words really do by nature is used

explanation.surface: Some people genuinely, by nature, are lifted up by the Everyman crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the Observer's crossword, but here it means the ordinary person.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyman is any ordinary person, and anybody means any person at all.

clue.text: Spooner derides brown cowboy

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the starting sounds of words, as this clue asks

parts.note: to deride is to mock, so derides gives mocks; said quickly its final s slides onto the next word
tan is a light brown colour, heard with the s carried over from the word before

explanation.surface: A cowboy is ridiculed for his suntan.
explanation.walkthrough: Say MOCKS TAN as MOCK STAN, then swap the opening M and ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockman looks after livestock, especially cattle on a ranch, much as a cowboy does.

clue.text: Furthest off the mark with last two in Toughie

parts.note: the final two letters of Toughie are IE, the abbreviation for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Being the most wrong at the end of the Telegraph's Toughie crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: The Toughie is the Daily Telegraph's harder crossword. IE is the abbreviation of the Latin id est, written out here in full.
explanation.definitionFit: The widest shot misses the target by the greatest margin, wide meaning off target.

clue.text: Awful systems — nothing odd here — create ineffectual people

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are dropped, keeping the even ones

explanation.surface: Terrible systems produce feeble people.
explanation.definitionFit: Wusses are weaklings or wimps, people lacking strength or courage.

clue.text: Age of bird, not beast

indicators.note: the beast is not included, so it is taken out of the bird

parts.note: a pigeon is a bird
a pig is a beast

explanation.surface: Asking a bird's age, not an animal's.
explanation.definitionFit: An eon is an immensely long stretch of time, an age.

clue.text: Solver seen in agony — ouch!

indicators.note: the letters can be seen inside the words agony ouch

explanation.surface: A puzzle-solver in pain, crying out.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often address the solver as you.
explanation.definitionFit: The person reading the clue is the solver, addressed as the second person.

clue.text: Stripped of flesh, act fatal: icy tombs found here

definitions.text: Stripped of flesh, act fatal: icy tombs found here

indicators.note: each word loses its outer layer, leaving only the inner letters

explanation.surface: A grim picture of skeletons laid out in cold underground tombs.
explanation.definitionFit: Catacombs are underground cemeteries where bodies were laid in tombs in the rock.

clue.text: Both Telegraph and Herald are noteworthy

definitions.meaning: to telegraph is to ..., give a sign in advance
to herald is to ... the coming of something
... as an adjective means remarkable, as in a ... achievement

explanation.surface: Two newspaper titles are both declared remarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: Telegraph and Herald look like newspapers; they are verbs here.
explanation.definitionFit: Signal works as a verb for giving a warning sign and as an adjective meaning striking or remarkable.

clue.text: Good! One newspaper has flair

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
FT is the Financial Times newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone praises a newspaper for its style.
explanation.definitionFit: A gift is a natural talent, much like a flair for something.

clue.text: What the Inquisitor does: challenges where you must set aside time

indicators.note: the time abbreviation is put to one side, removed

parts.note: tasks are challenges to be done

explanation.surface: The Inquisitor crossword sets challenges you must find time for.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inquisitor is the i newspaper's hard crossword, but as a questioner an inquisitor simply asks.
explanation.definitionFit: An inquisitor questions people, so what one does is pose questions.

clue.text: One challenges you to give in, taking on Observer, say

indicators.note: the word for give in takes on another letter inside it

parts.note: to defer is to yield to someone
an observer is an eye, which sounds like I

explanation.surface: A rival dares you to surrender, recruiting the Observer newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer looks like the Sunday paper; here an observer is an eye, said aloud as I.
explanation.definitionFit: A defier is someone who openly resists or challenges authority or another person.

clue.text: Video deception by leaders in dubiously elected executive presidencies fooling all, kindling enmity

indicators.note: takes the first letter of each of the following words

parts.words: dubiously elected executive presidencies fooling all, kindling enmity

explanation.surface: Fake videos of shady presidents stir up hatred and fool everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: A deepfake is a digitally manipulated video making someone appear to say or do what they did not.
